The word hazard here describes a change in behavior, not a moral defect; the response is a rational one to altered incentives. Insurers have developed familiar tools in response. Deductibles and copayments ensure that the insured keeps a stake in the outcome; premiums that fall for a record of safe driving reward careful behavior; and screening, such as a medical examination, narrows the information gap before a policy is issued.

Each remedy has a cost, however. A high deductible reduces moral hazard but also exposes people to the very financial risk they sought to escape, and there is evidence that it discourages them from seeking beneficial care along with unnecessary care. Screening can protect the insurer, but it may leave the people with the greatest needs uninsured, defeating the purpose of the arrangement. For this reason, many governments have chosen to mandate coverage for everyone. A compulsory scheme eliminates adverse selection, since the healthy cannot leave, but it requires a political willingness to compel participation and subsidize those who cannot afford the premium, and it leaves moral hazard to be addressed by other means.

The two problems are often discussed as if they were separate defects of insurance, but they share a source: the person insured knows something, whether about his health or about his intentions, that the insurer cannot observe. Both are reminders that a market is more than a meeting of buyers and sellers with settled preferences. It is also a system for conveying information, and where information cannot be conveyed the market does not simply perform poorly; it may fail to exist. The design of institutions that do the conveying, through contracts, regulations, or compulsory pooling, is among the central tasks of applied economics.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Gaps in information between insurers and buyers create problems that can undermine insurance markets and require institutional solutions.
options.B: Insurance markets function best when buyers and sellers have identical information and settled preferences.
options.C: Mandatory insurance is the only remedy for the problems created by moral hazard.
options.D: Moral hazard arises because people who purchase insurance are morally defective.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The final paragraph traces both problems to an information gap and describes institutions as the remedy. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says information is what a market must convey, but not that equality of information is always achieved. C) Mandates address adverse selection, and the passage says they leave moral hazard to be handled otherwise. D) The author explicitly says that hazard refers to behavior, not a defect.
questions.trap: Taking one remedy (mandates) as the central subject.

questions.stem: The used-car example is included in the passage in order to:

options.A: show that insurers should avoid selling coverage to owners of used cars.
options.B: illustrate that adverse selection can occur in markets other than insurance.
options.C: demonstrate that moral hazard is the reason that good cars disappear from the market.
options.D: argue that buyers should never purchase used goods.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Buyers who cannot tell good from bad pay an average price, which drives out sellers of good cars, as healthy people leave an insurance pool. Why the others are wrong: A) The example is an analogy, not advice to insurers. C) The example concerns adverse selection, which happens before the sale. D) The author gives no advice on purchasing used goods.
questions.trap: Missing the analogy and confusing the two problems.

questions.stem: A car owner who has full coverage begins parking in unsafe areas because he will not pay for any theft. This best illustrates:

options.A: adverse selection, because the owner knew more about his risks than the insurer did.
options.B: screening, because the insurer has narrowed the information gap.
options.C: a deductible, because the insured keeps a stake in the outcome.
options.D: moral hazard, because the insured changes his behavior after being protected.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Moral hazard is a change in behavior after a policy is sold in response to altered incentives. Why the others are wrong: A) Adverse selection occurs before a policy is sold. B) Screening occurs before issuing the policy and he did not cause it. C) A deductible would give him a stake; he has none.
questions.trap: Confusing the pre-sale and post-sale problems.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that mandatory coverage eliminates adverse selection?

options.A: Governments that mandate coverage must subsidize premiums for people who cannot afford them.
options.B: Mandatory coverage leaves moral hazard to be addressed by other means.
options.C: High deductibles discourage people from seeking beneficial as well as unnecessary care.
options.D: Many healthy people can remain uninsured under the mandate without penalty.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The claim depends on the healthy being unable to leave the pool; if they can remain uninsured, the pool would still skew toward the sick. Why the others are wrong: A) Subsidies are a cost of the scheme the author already notes, not a challenge to the mechanism. B) The author already acknowledges this limit, and it concerns moral hazard. C) This concerns deductibles, not mandates.
questions.trap: Selecting costs the author already admits.

questions.stem: The author's statement that where information cannot be conveyed a market 'may fail to exist' is most directly supported by which example in the passage?

options.A: The use of deductibles to keep the insured invested in outcomes.
options.B: The collapse of the pool as healthy customers leave and premiums rise.
options.C: Reduced premiums for a record of safe driving.
options.D: The requirement that governments subsidize premiums for people who cannot afford coverage on their own.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The extreme case of adverse selection is a collapsed market in which the needy cannot buy coverage at any affordable price. Why the others are wrong: A) Deductibles are a remedy for moral hazard. C) Safe-driving discounts reward behavior after sale. D) Subsidies are part of a mandate, which solves the problem.
questions.trap: Choosing a remedy rather than the failure the statement describes.
